title: Managed endpoint win themes playbook for cloud AI platforms
body:
Purpose:
Quick internal playbook for PMM/Sales/SEs to position Redwood versus cloud provider managed endpoints (AWS/GCP/Azure). Focus is on pragmatic win themes, likely objections, and short scripts for discovery and demo framing. Working doc — please add notes, especially battle-test lines from customer calls.

Audience:
- Platform engineers evaluating managed endpoints for production LLM features
- ML infra leads who care about cost and latency at scale
- Security/compliance stakeholders comparing private deployments and data residency

Top-line positioning (single-sentence hooks):
- For engineers who need predictable, low-latency LLM inference across hosted and private environments, Redwood provides a single runtime and controls (dedicated pools, caching, quantization) that reduce per-token spend and keep apps online even when cloud endpoints degrade.
- Unlike hyperscaler managed endpoints that prioritize convenience inside their cloud, Redwood focuses on inference economics, multi-environment consistency, and production-grade fallbacks.

Competitive landscape summary (high level):
- AWS (SageMaker Endpoints / Bedrock): strong cloud integrations, broad ecosystem, built-in scaling. Common pain: opaque per-token cost at high QPS, limited private-tenant runtimes, fallbacks across regions/providers hard to implement.
- GCP (Vertex AI / Model Garden): excellent for data integration (BigQuery, Dataflow), good MLOps tooling. Pain: endpoint cost + latency when traffic spikes, fewer fine-grained runtime controls for batching/kv-caching, private air-gapped options limited.
- Azure (Azure OpenAI / Managed Endpoints): enterprise-friendly with Microsoft stack, good compliance posture. Pain: vendor lock-in concerns, limited direct control over quantization/prod batching knobs, often expensive for high-throughput generation.

Key technical differentiators to call out (what SEs should emphasize):
1) Unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private: same API and rollout mechanics whether customer uses Redwood Hosted or a VPC/on-prem tenant. Cuts integration risk and testing overhead.
2) Cost controls at token level: per-route batching suggestions, KV/prefix caching, and quantization recommendations tied to real customer token distributions — measurable unit economics improvements.
3) Reliability with graceful degradation: automated routing/fallback policies to cheaper model variants, region failover, and reserved dedicated pools to avoid noisy-neighbor tail latency.
4) Production telemetry and observability: token-level cost/latency breakdowns, per-model regressions tied to evals/prompt sets, and tracing hooks to connect inference events to app traces.
5) Private deployment support: VPC control plane, on-prem packaging, and KMS/HSM integration for regulated customers — offered with enterprise SLAs.

Common customer pain signals (discovery prompts):
- "Our endpoint costs balloon when traffic spikes — can you show cost savings at QPS X?"
- "We need sub-100ms tail latency for chat — do you guarantee that at scale?"
- "We must keep inference inside our VPC/on-prem for compliance — what options do you have?"
- "We want consistent behavior across dev/prod and between cloud/on-prem; right now results drift between endpoints."

Direct win themes vs each provider (script snippets):
- Against AWS/GCP/Azure managed endpoints: "If you need tight control over serving economics and predictable latency at production QPS — especially across hybrid or multi-cloud footprints — Redwood is built for that. Our dedicated pools and runtime-level caching mean you often pay less per successful response while keeping tail latency under your SLOs."
- Against hyperscaler convenience: "Hyperscalers are great early on. Once you cross a usage threshold, you’ll want precise levers to tune cost/latency tradeoffs without rewriting code — that’s where Redwood sits."

Objection handling (short):
- Objection: "We already use SageMaker/Vertex/Azure and want to stay inside the cloud."
  Response: "We integrate with cloud infra and can run private control planes in the same region — you get the operational simplicity you want plus the production inference controls you need. Many customers start with hosted Redwood and later run Dedicated in their cloud account."
- Objection: "Isn’t this just another wrapper around model servers?"
  Response: "It’s more: runtime-level optimizations (continuous batching, KV cache, quantization-aware execution) plus orchestration that manages model variants, rollouts, and automated fallbacks. Those features materially change token economics and reliability at scale."

Demo checklist (what to show in a 20–30m seat):
- Quick baseline: show same prompt against a hyperscaler endpoint and Redwood-hosted. Emphasize latency and token economics (if allowed).
- Dedicated capacity: show traffic shaping/guarantees and burst behavior.
- Routing/fallback: simulate capacity drop and show automatic fallback to compatible model variant.
- Cost/observability: token-level breakdowns, per-route heatmaps, and an eval regression alert firing.
- Private deployment brief: architecture sketch (VPC, KMS, audit logs).

Battlecard bullets for SDR/AE (30–60s soundbites):
- "Redwood reduces per-token cost via batching, caching and smart kernel selection — customers see up to 3x effective throughput in many inference workloads."
- "We provide consistent APIs across hosted, dedicated, and private — no code changes for different deployment modes."
- "Run inference where you need it: public cloud, dedicated reserved pools, or inside your VPC/on-prem with enterprise security controls."

Pricing/ROI framing guidance (how to position):
- Use committed capacity comparisons for Dedicated vs cloud managed endpoints at target QPS. Frame as: committed price + predictable throughput vs hyperscaler dynamic pricing that spikes.
- Talk about total cost of ownership (TCO): show savings from reduced token usage (caching/batching) + lower ops time because rollouts & tracing are built-in.

Collateral recommendations (short list to produce):
- Two-pager: "Managed Endpoints Comparison — When to go Redwood vs Hyperscaler" (customer-facing brief)
- SE playbook: demo scripts + CLI snippets to show dedicated provisioning and fallback tests
- ROI calculator spreadsheet pre-populated for typical chat/assistant workloads (QPS, avg tokens, expected latency)
- One-page private-deployment checklist for security/compliance teams

Open questions / TODOs (working):
- Get up-to-date public pricing comparisons for SageMaker, Vertex, Azure Managed Endpoints for main regions (US-EAST, EU-WEST). TODO: Maya to pull these by 2024-11-25.
- Collect 3 anonymized case studies where customers moved off hyperscaler endpoints for cost/perf reasons. TODO: Ravi to source from CS.
- Validate quantization performance claims on recent open models (Llama2-13B/30B distros). TODO: Bench team to run 4k token sequences.

Tone and voice guidance for messaging:
- Engineer-first, numbers-focused, pragmatic (avoid marketing hyperbole).
- Use concrete levers (batching configs, KV cache, model variants, reserved pools) not generic adjectives.
- Always map a capability to a developer/infra outcome (e.g., "reduces tail latency" -> "keeps chat sessions snappy for end users when traffic spikes").

Appendix: Quick competitive factoids (for SE referee):
- Hyperscalers: strong native platform integrations (IAM, storage, data pipelines) and heavy investment in data labeling and MLOps; Redwood complements those strengths by focusing on serving economics and fallback reliability across environments.
- Typical hyperscaler weakness: limited knobs exposed to tune inference kernels/quantization at runtime; limited cross-region/fallback automation for model variants.
